analysis.title: GLP-1s: A Health Revolution at What Cost?
key_insights: GLP-1 receptor agonists could be the next structural shift in population health, with potential to transform treatment of diabetes, obesity and associated chronic diseases including cardiovascular and kidney disease.
Open question is whether GLP-1s extend healthspan, lifespan or both. Longer life with more years managing illness would raise pension and insurance liabilities with little productivity offset.

GLP-1s may reshape the healthcare cost curve rather than lower it. Spending shifts from lumpy, back-loaded acute care to smooth, front-loaded drug spend across a much larger treated population. Net savings depend on drug price and adherence.

Payer and beneficiary are often different in fragmented systems such as the US. A private insurer pays for the drug while avoided late-life costs accrue to Medicare, Medicaid or the state, which explains restrictive private reimbursement.
In single-payer systems (UK NHS, Gulf states) payer and beneficiary are more likely the same, which favours adoption, but near-term budget impact still forces rationing.
US adoption: about 12% of adults currently use a GLP-1 and 18% have ever used one. Use peaks at ages 50-64. More than half of users report affordability difficulties.
Persistence is weak: 53.6% of US adults prescribed a GLP-1 discontinued at one year and 72.2% at two years, due to side effects, cost and non-adherence. GI side effects affect up to 60% of patients.
Patent expiry is expected in the early-to-mid 2030s, with the patent waterfall running to 2035-40. Generics and compounders could cut costs and widen access.
Statin precedent: 20-year forecasts across major developed countries underestimated life expectancy by about three years on average. GLP-1 uptake is faster than statins.

Man argues the largest liability shock may land on state pay-as-you-go pensions, public sector DB schemes and social security if access widens to less affluent populations. Wealthy insured groups already in pension and insurance books suggest a manageable, possibly underpriced medium-term shock.
Emerging markets could see the systemic longevity signal first: China and India together have close to 600 million overweight or obese adults, with weaker public-health financing.
Timing asymmetry: longer lifespan raises liabilities immediately, while healthspan productivity gains accrue over decades, if at all.

Insurance: allocators should check whether insurers and reinsurers are updating mortality improvement assumptions and building GLP-1-aware underwriting. Man suggests owning institutions that reprice longevity risk correctly. Net effect for diversified insurers is ambiguous.
Pension funds facing funding-ratio erosion could become forced sellers of assets, hurting prices and liquidity for co-investors.
Possible opportunities: liability-driven investment demand for long-dated bonds if DB funds extend duration, and distressed pension risk transfer, insurance or infrastructure assets.

Sector effects: consumer staples (processed food, alcohol demand), pharma (as the class matures and generics enter), senior living and care homes, with lower acute hospital demand and higher community and rehab demand.

Indicators to watch: GLP-1 prescription volumes, adherence, coverage decisions (1-3 years); generic pipeline and healthspan/sarcopenia data (3-6 years); official mortality assumption revisions and DB funding ratios (7-14 years).

sector_views.rationale: Demand for processed meals and alcohol could fall as habits change with GLP-1 use. Man flags this as an exposure, not a call.
Exposure shifts as the GLP-1 class matures and generic makers and compounders enter after 2030s patent expiries.

sector_views.sector: Senior living and healthcare real estate
sector_views.rationale: Lifespan extension affects demand for care homes, retirement villages, senior living REITs and healthcare facilities. Acute hospital demand may fall while community and rehab demand rises.
Life insurers may gain from lower mortality, but annuity, DB and longevity-risk books lose if people live longer. Net effect is ambiguous for diversified insurers.

macro_indicators.reading: 2.1 billion in 2021, projected almost 3.8 billion by 2050
macro_indicators.interpretation: Large treatable population underpins long-run GLP-1 demand and the associated fiscal exposure.

macro_indicators.reading: up to US$1.6 trillion annually by 2035 in upper middle-income countries; global GDP reduction of about 2.9% (~US$4 trillion)
macro_indicators.interpretation: Sets the scale of the potential offset if GLP-1s reduce obesity-related disease.

risk_factors: Mortality improvement assumptions in pension and insurance models may be too low, producing unmodelled liability shocks.
Longer lifespan without matching healthspan raises pension liabilities with no productivity offset.
State PAYG pensions, public sector DB schemes and social security face the largest potential shock if access widens to excluded populations.
Pension funds with eroding funding ratios may become forced sellers of assets.
Loss of lean mass (sarcopenia), frailty and GI side effects may limit benefits and persistence.
Negative EVOKE/EVOKE+ semaglutide Alzheimer's trial results (November 2025) cut against broader healthspan claims.
geopolitical: US government pricing agreements with Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly for Medicare and Medicaid obesity drug coverage (6 November 2025 White House fact sheet), with a temporary CMS demonstration running to end-2027.

tension_points.bull_case: If GLP-1s extend healthspan, longer working lives, higher productivity, lower healthcare, disability and long-term care costs could partly offset pension and annuity liabilities.
tension_points.bear_case: If people live longer with comorbidities such as muscle loss, pension liabilities rise with little productivity offset. Lifespan gains raise liabilities immediately while healthspan savings accrue over decades, if at all.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Long-term evidence on years lived in good health, such as sarcopenia and healthspan trial data, and official mortality improvement assumption revisions. The report calls the latter probably the most important indicator.

theme_stances.key_argument: Longer lifespans immediately raise pension and annuity obligations while productivity savings from better health accrue only over decades, if at all.
theme_stances.evidence: one that the financial system has not yet priced-in
